title: Volume of cylinders
log: 2026-11-04T09:36:57Z match: Claude Haiku 5.5 found no bank point the same, so it is written new

match.reason: The closest bank point, mat-volume-capacity, is broader than this point: it covers all prisms and capacity conversions and is written for Year 11 NSW and Units 1 and 2 Victoria, so it does not match the narrower Year 9 cylinder-volume idea.

draft.title: Volume of cylinders
card: Volume is the amount of space inside a solid. It is measured in cubic units, such as cm³.
A cylinder has a circle as its base. The area of the base is πr², where r is the radius.
Volume = base area × height, so V = πr²h. Square the radius first, then multiply by π and by the height.
Example: r = 3 cm and h = 10 cm. V = π × 3² × 10 = π × 9 × 10 = 90π, which is about 283 cm³.
draft.remember: Volume of a cylinder is the circle's area times the height.

a.q: A cylinder has radius 2 cm and height 5 cm. What is its volume, in terms of π?
a.why: V = π × 2² × 5 = π × 4 × 5 = 20π cm³. 10π comes from multiplying r by h without squaring r, which is a common slip.
a.clue: Square the radius before you multiply.

b.q: A water tank is a cylinder with diameter 4 m and height 3 m. What is its volume, to the nearest cubic metre?
b.why: The radius is half the diameter, so r = 2 m. V = π × 2² × 3 = 12π, which is about 38 m³. Using 4 as the radius gives 48π, about 151 m³, which is wrong.
b.clue: The diameter is not the radius.
